sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Go interfaces are the primary abstraction mechanism in the language and appear constantly in real codebases and in interviews. Unlike Java, Go uses implicit (structural) satisfaction — a type implements an interface simply by having the right methods, with no 'implements' keyword. Understanding this, along with the nil interface pitfall and how embedding enables composition over inheritance, separates junior from intermediate Go engineers.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: An interface value is a two-word structure: a type pointer and a data pointer. A non-nil interface can still have a nil data pointer if the concrete type stored inside is a nil pointer — this is the infamous nil interface pitfall. Struct embedding is not inheritance; it is syntactic sugar that promotes fields and methods to the outer type, but the embedded type has no knowledge of its host. Compose small interfaces (io.Reader, io.Writer) rather than fat ones, following the Go standard library's design.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
• Implicit satisfaction: no declaration needed; the compiler checks at the assignment site.
• empty interface / any: accepts any value, but you lose all static type information — use sparingly.
• Interface composition: embed multiple interfaces to build larger contracts (io.ReadWriter).
• Struct embedding: promoted methods satisfy interfaces automatically; useful for decorator patterns.
• fmt.Stringer and error: two most common single-method interfaces; know how to implement them.
• Nil interface pitfall: (*T)(nil) stored in an interface is not == nil; always return a bare nil interface, not a typed nil pointer.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
• 'How does Go achieve polymorphism without inheritance?' — interfaces and composition via embedding.
• 'What is the difference between a nil interface and an interface holding a nil pointer?' — classic trap question.
• 'When would you use any vs a typed interface?' — JSON unmarshalling, generic containers, reflection.
• 'Can embedding cause method ambiguity? How is it resolved?' — yes; outermost type wins, or compiler error if depth is equal.
• 'Why does Go prefer small interfaces?' — easier to satisfy, more composable, simpler to mock in tests.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "Go interfaces are structural, not nominal — a type satisfies an interface the moment it has the right method set, with no explicit declaration. I find this makes testing much cleaner because I can wrap any third-party type in a thin interface and swap in a mock without changing the production code. The one footgun I always watch for is the nil interface pitfall: if I return a *MyError typed nil inside a function that returns error, the caller's nil check will fail because the interface value carries type information. The fix is to return an untyped nil at the return statement. For composition I reach for struct embedding — it promotes methods to the outer type and often lets me satisfy an interface without writing any delegation boilerplate."
